title: Iridium 33 x Cosmos 2251

facts.text: From 4 February, all 14 reports of the free SOCRATES screening (public TLE data) predicted an Iridium 33 x Cosmos 2251 approach at the collision time, between 117 m and 1.8 km. None made its Top Ten.
Iridium 33 had 10 to 15 predicted approaches within 5 km every week. With TLE data, this one could not be told apart from the rest.
Iridium planned a routine station-keeping maneuver for Iridium 33.

At 07:10 and 08:00 UTC, two hydrazine burns of 0.0022 m/s raised its orbit by 8.3 m, onto Cosmos 2251's path. Iridium could not see the military's precise catalog; the military did not know about the burn.
The last SOCRATES report, at 15:02 UTC, predicted a 584 m miss and ranked the approach 152nd.
At 16:55:59.8 UTC, Iridium 33 (operational) and Cosmos 2251 (defunct since about 1995) collided at 11.6 km/s over Siberia. Both were destroyed.

aftermath.text: Iridium and the US military agreed to share data: Iridium sends planned maneuvers, the military returns daily screenings with covariance.
In one week the debris produced 629 predicted approaches within 5 km with Iridium and Orbcomm satellites.
US military screening grew from about 120 to about 1,150 active satellites.
The International Space Station changed its orbit to avoid a piece of Iridium 33 debris.
NASA: 2,201 fragments catalogued from the collision, 1,821 still in orbit.
Iridium replayed the archived data: merged, it showed the risk days ahead. In its words, "no one shared their bucket".

debris.modelMethod: NASA standard breakup model, fragments >= 10 cm

assumptions: Encounter reconstructed from published values, not from historical element sets: circular orbits at 789 km (Wikipedia), inclinations 86 and 74 deg (Kelso, Table 1), crossing chosen for the published 11.6 km/s relative speed (model: 11.59 km/s).
They collided, so the predicted miss on the planned trajectory is modelled as 0 m (a direct hit).

Covariance: Iridium 33 uses Iridium's own conservative model, R/T/N = 20 / 120*dt+60 / 20 m (Shepperd), (20, 165, 20) m at 0.87 days; Cosmos 2251 (30.0, 300.0, 50.0) m (not published; assumption). Combined in the encounter plane: 219 x 36 m.
Hard-body radius 19.9 m: Iridium 33 3.942 m + Cosmos 2251 16 m, as in Iridium's replay (Shepperd).

Planning time 09 Feb 20:00 UTC, the day the station-keeping burn was planned (Shepperd). Policy as for live events: burn when Pc >= 0.0001, target Pc <= 1e-07 and miss >= 1000 m (app.physics.maneuver).
Iridium 33: 556 kg dry mass (Kelso, Table 1; propellant left in 2009 is unknown, so this is a lower bound) and hydrazine thrusters (Shepperd) at an assumed Isp of 220 s.
The burn is rounded up to the planner's 0.01 m/s grid, so the real minimum may be smaller.
Debris model: NASA standard breakup model for a catastrophic collision of 556 + 900 kg at 11.6 km/s, fragments >= 10 cm (app.physics.cascade).
Pc over time is quoted from Iridium's replay (Shepperd, Table 2, Foster method), not computed here. The 10 Feb one-sided value used knowledge of Iridium's burn to shorten the orbit fit.
